title: Omo Tuo with Seven Cups of Water
author: Rachel Ofori
desc: The wettest of the three — three cups of rice to seven of water, twenty to twenty-five minutes, mashed smooth rather than mushy.
longDesc: This version takes the rice much further than the others: seven cups of water to three of rice, well over twice the usual ratio, cooked low and covered for twenty to twenty-five minutes until very soft. Where the other documented versions warn against a smooth mash, this one asks for it directly — mash the rice until smooth while it is still hot, then form medium-sized balls with wet hands. Whether that is a different technique or a different idea of the dish is not settled by any source, so both are published.
ingredients: 3 cups rice — the type is not specified
equipment: Bowl of water, for wetting the hands
steps: Rinse the rice thoroughly under cold water.
In a pot, bring the water to the boil.
Add the salt and the rice.
Reduce the heat to low, cover, and cook about 20 to 25 minutes, until the rice is very soft.
While the rice is still hot, use a wooden spoon or a rice paddle to mash it until smooth.
Wet your hands with water and form the mashed rice into medium-sized balls.
chefTips: Seven cups to three is more than twice the water of the driest documented version. If you have had omo tuo collapse into soup, this ratio is why it might instead have been too dry to bind.
This source asks for smooth, where another insists on mushy-not-mashed. Both are published and neither is wrong — decide which texture you actually want before you start mashing.
Low and covered for the full twenty to twenty-five minutes. At this much water, high heat will boil over.
Mash while hot, which all three versions agree on. It is the one point of consensus.
Medium-sized balls, formed with wet hands. Large ones do not hold.
The rice type is not stated here, unlike the two versions that specify jasmine. A long grain will behave differently from jasmine at this hydration.
If the finished mass is too loose to shape, there is no published remedy — cook the next batch drier rather than trying to rescue this one.
commonMistakes: Treating seven cups as a misprint and reducing it without testing.
High heat under a very wet pot.
Balls too large to hold together.
Assuming jasmine rice when the source does not specify a type.
sources: Adapted from 'Omo Tuo and Nkate Nkwan — Rice Balls and Groundnut Soup', lecreuset.co.uk. CREDIT AS PRINTED: 'Recipe by Rachel @tastycurls.' BYLINE FLAG: that is a social-media handle with no surname, and the host is a cookware retailer's site rather than a publication. Both are recorded. Yield as printed: 'SERVES 4-6'.
Quantities exactly as printed, TWO-PASS consistent: '3 cups rice'; '7 cups water'; 'Pinch of salt'. THE RICE TYPE IS NOT SPECIFIED, unlike the two other documented versions which both name jasmine.

Method verbatim: 'Rinse the rice thoroughly under cold water. In a pot, bring the water to a boil.' Add salt and rice. 'Reduce the heat to low, cover, and cook for about 20-25 minutes until the rice is very soft.' 'While the rice is still hot, use a wooden spoon or a rice paddle to mash the rice until smooth.' 'Wet your hands with water and form the mashed rice into medium-sized balls.'

PAGE FLAG: the method steps are numbered 16 to 20 on the page, which means the printed recipe is a fragment of a longer combined omo-tuo-and-groundnut-soup method. Nothing appears to be missing from the rice steps themselves, but the numbering is recorded in case the page is revised.

THE 7:3 RATIO IS NOT TREATED AS A MISPRINT and has not been adjusted. It is roughly 2.33 cups of water per cup of rice against 1.5 in the Savory Thoughts version (GHA003) and 1.75 in Nanasei Agyemang's (GHA005). All three are published side by side rather than averaged, because at this hydration the resulting texture is genuinely a different thing.

THE TEXTURE CONTRADICTION, unreconciled: this source says mash 'until smooth'. The Savory Thoughts version says explicitly that it should NOT look like mashed potatoes and should be 'mushy but not "mashed"'. Two named sources asking for two different textures under one dish name; neither is corrected.
No doneness cue beyond 'very soft' and the time window. No sensory endpoint is given.
The same page carries a groundnut soup to go with these rice balls; see GHA015 and GHA016 for the documented groundnut soups.
reheating: Steam, or drop into hot soup.
healthBenefits: Very soft and easy to digest.
No added sugar; salt is only a pinch.
culturalNote: That the clearest omo tuo quantities in print come from a cookware retailer's recipe page, credited to a social handle, says something about how this dish has been documented. It is eaten every Sunday by millions of people and almost nobody has written down how much water to use — which is why all three versions here are published rather than reconciled.
